input.query: Do the authors offer a hypothesis for why Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country in 'Mapping Languages and Demographics with Georeferenced Corpora'?

output.reason: The evidence supports a 'yes' answer. The Discussion section offers hypotheses for why Twitter differs from web-crawled data: Twitter matches populations better when weighted by GDP and worse by internet-usage statistics, implying Twitter represents wealthier populations, and an alternate interpretation is that the Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to be wealthier. The evidence also notes Twitter has fewer missing languages (fewer false negatives) and that English/Spanish are very common on Twitter, aiding representation. However, the evidence does not explicitly state these as the reason for the specific claim 'Twitter makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country,' but it does provide hypotheses about Twitter's representativeness and fewer missing languages, which directly relate to the language inventory prediction.

claims.text: The abstract states that Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country.
The discussion reports that Twitter has fewer missing languages than the web-crawled corpus in representing all languages produced by local populations.

The authors note that both corpora agree on predictions for Europe, parts of Africa with ground-truth data, and South America, but Twitter provides a better representation of North America and Oceania.

The authors caution that many countries have only a few languages, so a high true positive rate may reflect only one or two languages; since English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, countries predominantly using these languages will have good representation by default.

Regarding why Twitter and web-crawled data represent different populations, the authors suggest that Twitter data matches populations better when weighted by GDP and worse when weighted by internet-usage statistics, implying Twitter represents more wealthy populations; they also offer an alternate interpretation that their Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to have wealthier populations.
The authors state that more research is needed to distinguish between immigration, tourism, and business as alternate sources of false positive languages appearing in digital data sets.
